steps.prompt: What’s the difference in time between these two sentences?
steps.a: When Mom got home, we cleaned the kitchen.
steps.b: When Mom got home, we had cleaned the kitchen.
steps.reveal: In the first, we started cleaning when Mom arrived. In the second, the kitchen was already clean when she walked in: “had cleaned” shows it happened first. Perfect and progressive tenses let you show exactly how actions line up in time.

cards.title: Progressive: in progress
cards.body: A progressive verb shows an action that is (or was, or will be) going on: a form of be + an -ing verb. Present: “I am reading.” Past: “We were waiting when the bus came.” Future: “She will be playing at noon.”

cards.title: Perfect: completed before a time
cards.body: A perfect verb shows an action finished before a certain time: has/have/had + the past participle. Present perfect links the past to now: “I have visited Texas twice.” Past perfect shows the earlier of two past actions: “The show had started when we arrived.” Future perfect: “By June, I will have finished.”

cards.title: The verb tense grid
cards.text:
Simple: I walk · I walked · I will walk
Progressive: I am walking · I was walking · I will be walking
Perfect: I have walked · I had walked · I will have walked
cards.note: Three times (present, past, future) × three kinds (simple, progressive, perfect). The helping verb shows the time; the main verb’s ending shows the kind.

cards.title: Which happened first?
cards.telling: I finished my homework when Dad called me for dinner.
cards.showing: I had finished my homework when Dad called me for dinner.
cards.note: Use “had” + participle for the action that happened first. It’s a big help when you explain events in an essay.

prompts: Explain the difference between “I was eating” and “I had eaten” to a friend.
Where could the past perfect help you explain events in an essay?
